questions.text: "It is clear ___ disinformation is a growing threat to democratic discourse." (noun clause)
questions.hint: "It is clear that + clause"

questions.text: "Researchers have found ___ corrections reach far fewer people than the original false claims."
questions.hint: "Found that + clause" — reporting verb + that-clause

questions.text: "___ concerns me most is the concentration of media ownership in a few wealthy hands."
questions.hint: "What + S + V + is + X" = wh-clause as grammatical subject

questions.text: "The fact ___ the story was fabricated was established within 24 hours by multiple fact-checkers."
questions.hint: "The fact that + clause" — noun phrase + that-clause

questions.text: "She realised ___ the account she had been following was automated — a bot."
questions.hint: "Realised that + clause" — cognitive verb + that-clause

questions.text: "The debate about ___ platforms should bear legal responsibility for content is intensifying."
questions.hint: After prepositions: "whether" not "if"

questions.text: "I wonder ___ social media companies have done enough to combat disinformation."
questions.hint: "Wonder whether/if" = embedded yes/no question

questions.text: "Can you tell me ___ the website publishes credible reporting?" (embedded yes/no question)
questions.hint: Both "if" and "whether" are acceptable in mid-sentence embedded yes/no questions

questions.text: "She couldn't decide ___ share the unverified story or wait for confirmation." (choice with infinitive)
questions.hint: "Couldn't decide whether to + infinitive" — no subject after "whether to"

questions.text: "Researchers are investigating ___ filter bubbles reduce exposure to opposing viewpoints."
questions.hint: "Investigating whether" = embedded yes/no question

questions.text: What is the difference between misinformation and disinformation?
opts: Misinformation uses bots; disinformation uses humans
Disinformation is deliberately spread to deceive; misinformation is not necessarily intentional
Misinformation is more dangerous than disinformation
questions.correct: Disinformation is deliberately spread to deceive; misinformation is not necessarily intentional
questions.hint: Reading 1: key distinction

questions.text: "I don't understand ___ this false story gained so much traction so quickly." (mechanism)
questions.hint: "How + S + V" = the mechanism/way — embedded wh-question

questions.text: "___ this widespread problem is has not yet been fully explained." (= the origin of the problem — wh-subject)
questions.hint: "Where + S + V" as a subject noun clause = the origin

questions.text: "She asked ___ did the fact-checker find." — What is wrong?
opts: "did the fact-checker find" should be "the fact-checker found"
questions.correct: "did the fact-checker find" should be "the fact-checker found"
questions.hint: No auxiliary inversion in embedded questions

questions.text: What is "lateral reading" according to the dialogue?
opts: Reading one article very carefully from start to finish
Searching for what other sources say about a source or claim
Comparing two news articles side by side
Reading a translated version of an article
questions.correct: Searching for what other sources say about a source or claim
questions.hint: Listening 3: Davyd explains lateral reading

questions.text: "It has been established ___ newsrooms without adequate funding produce less investigative journalism."
questions.hint: "It has been established that + clause" — passive reporting + noun clause

questions.text: "___ whether the accounts are bots or real users is a significant technical challenge." (subject clause)
questions.hint: Gerund + noun clause as subject: "Determining whether + S + V"

questions.text: "Despite the fact ___ the video was later debunked, it had already reached millions of people."
questions.hint: "Despite the fact that + clause"

questions.text: What is a "citation spiral" according to the dialogue?
opts: A legitimate network of independent sources
Multiple sites citing each other but all from one weak original source
A technique used by fact-checkers to verify claims
An algorithm that amplifies controversial content
questions.correct: Multiple sites citing each other but all from one weak original source
questions.hint: Listening 3: Davyd explains "citation spiral"

questions.text: "The question is not ___ action is needed, but ___ urgently we must act."
questions.hint: "Not whether… but how…" — two embedded questions for contrast and emphasis

questions.text: "Many doubt ___ self-regulation by technology platforms can adequately address disinformation."
questions.hint: "Doubt whether" = expressing doubt about a yes/no outcome

questions.text: A "news ___" is an area with no professional local news coverage.
questions.hint: Listening 3B: "news deserts"

questions.text: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
opts: "I wonder from where does it originate."
questions.hint: No inversion in embedded questions: "where + S + V"

questions.text: "Whether the site is reliable remains unclear" is grammatically correct (using "whether" as a subject clause).
questions.hint: "Whether + S + V" can be the subject of a sentence — "if" cannot

questions.text: What does "framing" mean in the context of media and propaganda?
opts: The physical layout of a news article
The way information is presented, which shapes its interpretation
A legal framework for regulating media
Adding visual images to news stories
questions.correct: The way information is presented, which shapes its interpretation
questions.hint: Reading 2: "framing — the way in which information is presented"
